title: Reproductive Pathogens
subject: Reproductive System (REPR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the organisms that cause sexually transmitted infections, vaginitis, toxic shock, and infections passed from mother to fetus or newborn. For each organism it explains structure, growth requirements, virulence factors, and how disease develops, then connects those features to the laboratory findings used to identify it: Gram stain, oxidase and sugar tests, selective media, dark-field microscopy, wet mount, KOH preparation, serology, and histology. Board questions usually present a smear, a culture result, a lesion, or a newborn finding and ask you to name the organism or explain the mechanism.
prerequisites: Bacterial cell envelope: gram-positive and gram-negative walls, peptidoglycan, lipopolysaccharide
Viral structure: envelope, capsid, and genome type
Antigen processing and presentation on MHC class II to CD4 T cells
Complement activation, opsonization, and the membrane attack complex
Cell cycle control by p53 and the retinoblastoma protein (Rb)

connections.how: This chapter's organisms illustrate IgA protease, complement evasion, superantigens, and placental transfer of IgG but not IgM.

connections.to: Pathology of the female genital tract
connections.how: High-risk HPV drives cervical intraepithelial neoplasia and carcinoma at the transformation zone.
The timing of fetal infection relative to organogenesis in weeks 3 to 8 explains why early TORCH infections cause structural defects.
HSV latency in sensory ganglia and the late neurologic lesions of syphilis link microbiology to the peripheral and central nervous systems.
Syphilitic aortitis and the patent ductus arteriosus of congenital rubella are cardiovascular outcomes of reproductive pathogens.

blocks.text: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative diplococcus whose paired cocci have flattened facing sides, giving a kidney bean shape. It infects only humans and dies quickly with drying or cold, so it spreads by direct mucosal contact during sex or from the birth canal to a newborn's eyes. It attaches to columnar and cuboidal epithelium (urethra, endocervix, rectum, pharynx, conjunctiva) rather than to the stratified squamous epithelium of the adult vagina.
Laboratory identification

Like all Neisseria, the gonococcus is oxidase positive and catalase positive. It produces acid from glucose but not maltose, while Neisseria meningitidis uses both, which is the classic way to separate the two. It is fastidious and grows best on chocolate agar in about 5% CO2. Thayer-Martin agar is chocolate agar with vancomycin (suppresses gram-positive organisms), colistin (suppresses most other gram-negative organisms), and nystatin (suppresses fungi), with trimethoprim added in the modified version to suppress Proteus, so commensals from genital, rectal, and pharyngeal sites do not overgrow it. In a man with urethral discharge, a Gram stain showing gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils is highly sensitive, but endocervical smears are much less reliable, so nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) is the usual test.

blocks.title: Gonococcal virulence factors
rows: Attach to nonciliated columnar cells; recombination of silent pilin copies into the expressed gene keeps changing pilin
No lasting immunity, frequent reinfection, no vaccine
Tight binding and entry into epithelial cells; switch on and off (phase variation)
Endotoxin with a short sugar chain instead of an O antigen; host sialic acid added to LOS resists complement
Neutrophil influx, purulent discharge, serum resistance
Cleaves secretory IgA1 at its hinge
Take iron directly from host proteins
blocks.caption: Unlike the meningococcus, the gonococcus has no polysaccharide capsule and depends on these surface factors.

blocks.title: From mucosal attachment to tubal scarring
steps: Pili attach to nonciliated columnar epithelial cells
Opa proteins mediate tight binding and transcytosis
Organisms reach subepithelial tissue
LOS and peptidoglycan fragments trigger TNF and neutrophils
Purulent urethritis or cervicitis
Ascent damages ciliated tubal cells: scarring, infertility, ectopic pregnancy
blocks.caption: Gonococcal disease is driven largely by the inflammatory response to LOS and released cell wall fragments.

blocks.text: Men usually have a purulent urethral discharge with dysuria. Women are often asymptomatic or have cervicitis, and ascending infection causes pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) and, occasionally, perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome). Neonatal conjunctivitis typically appears 2 to 5 days after birth. Bacteremic spread causes disseminated gonococcal infection with arthritis, tenosynovitis, and sparse pustular skin lesions. People lacking terminal complement components (C5 to C9) are prone to recurrent disseminated Neisseria infection because the membrane attack complex is the main way serum kills these organisms.

blocks.predict: A patient treated for gonorrhea last year is infected again by the same strain type. Why did the first infection not protect her?
blocks.explain: Pilin and Opa proteins change by recombination and phase variation, so antibodies made against last year's surface proteins no longer bind, and IgA protease degrades the mucosal antibody that remains.
blocks.check: The virulence factor table: pili, Opa, and IgA1 protease rows.

blocks.text: Chlamydia trachomatis is a small gram-negative-type bacterium that can grow only inside living host cells (obligate intracellular). It imports ATP from the host through an ATP/ADP exchange transporter and draws on host metabolites, so it does not grow on cell-free culture media. Its envelope has an outer membrane with lipopolysaccharide but very little peptidoglycan; the rigidity of the infectious form comes instead from outer membrane proteins cross-linked by disulfide bonds. The major outer membrane protein (MOMP) varies between strains and defines the serovars.

blocks.title: Chlamydial developmental cycle
steps: Elementary body attaches to a columnar epithelial cell
Enters by endocytosis; inclusion avoids lysosomal fusion
Elementary body converts to a reticulate body
Reticulate bodies divide by binary fission using host ATP
Reticulate bodies convert back to elementary bodies
Cell lysis or extrusion releases elementary bodies to infect new cells
blocks.caption: The cycle takes about 2 to 3 days. Only the elementary body is infectious; only the reticulate body divides.

blocks.text: The two forms suit two settings. The elementary body is small and tough enough to survive outside cells, while the reticulate body is fragile but metabolically active. Inclusions are seen in infected cells with Giemsa stain, and C. trachomatis inclusions contain glycogen that stains with iodine. Cell culture is possible but slow, so NAAT of urine or genital swabs is the standard diagnostic test. Much of the tissue damage comes from the host response: repeated or persistent infection drives chronic inflammation and scarring, which explains blinding trachoma and tubal infertility.

blocks.title: Serovars and their diseases
rows: Conjunctival epithelium; spread by hands, fomites, and flies
Trachoma: repeated follicular conjunctivitis, eyelid scarring, inturned lashes, corneal scarring, blindness
Urethritis, cervicitis, PID, epididymitis, proctitis, reactive arthritis; neonatal conjunctivitis (about 5 to 14 days) and afebrile pneumonia with staccato cough (about 4 to 12 weeks)
Lymphatics and mononuclear phagocytes in lymph nodes
Lymphogranuloma venereum: small painless ulcer, then painful inguinal nodes that may suppurate; proctocolitis
blocks.caption: Serovar differences in MOMP and tissue tropism explain why one species causes eye, genital, and lymphatic disease.

blocks.text: Genital infection with serovars D to K is often silent, especially in women, so ascending infection can scar the fallopian tubes before any symptoms prompt testing. LGV serovars are more invasive: they cross the epithelium, multiply in macrophages, and spread to regional nodes, producing granulomatous lymphadenitis. Because both chlamydia and gonorrhea cause urethritis, cervicitis, PID, and neonatal conjunctivitis, the timing of neonatal eye disease and the absence of organisms on Gram stain help point to Chlamydia.

Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum, the cause of syphilis, is a tightly coiled spirochete only about 0.1 to 0.2 micrometers wide. Its flagella lie in the periplasmic space between the inner and outer membranes (periplasmic flagella, or endoflagella), so the whole cell rotates like a corkscrew and can bore through viscous tissue and cross endothelium. Its outer membrane carries very few exposed proteins, which gives antibodies little to bind and helps the organism persist for years.

Because it is thinner than the resolving limit of ordinary light microscopy after Gram staining, it is seen by dark-field microscopy of fresh exudate from a chancre or condyloma latum, where it appears as a bright, motile spiral. Oral lesions are unsuitable because commensal mouth treponemes look the same. In tissue, silver stains or immunohistochemistry show it. It cannot be grown on standard laboratory media: it has a reduced genome, lacks many biosynthetic pathways, is microaerophilic, and divides only about once every 30 hours. Diagnosis therefore rests mainly on serology.

Transmission is by direct contact with moist primary or secondary lesions, and across the placenta at any stage of pregnancy. Fetal infection is most likely when maternal syphilis is early and organisms are abundant in the blood. The characteristic tissue lesion is endarteritis obliterans (concentric thickening of small arteries) with a plasma cell rich infiltrate, which explains the indurated chancre and the late damage to the aorta and nervous system.

blocks.title: Stages of acquired syphilis
rows: About 3 weeks after contact (range about 10 to 90 days)
Painless, indurated, clean-based chancre; painless rubbery regional nodes
Weeks to a few months later
Spirochetemia: rash including palms and soles, condylomata lata, generalized lymphadenopathy, fever
Gummas; aortitis from endarteritis of the vasa vasorum, causing ascending aortic aneurysm; tabes dorsalis and Argyll Robertson pupils
blocks.caption: Neurosyphilis can occur at any stage; tabes dorsalis is a late form.

blocks.title: Serologic tests
cols: Treponemal (FTA-ABS, TP-PA, enzyme or chemiluminescence immunoassays)
rows: Titer falls and often becomes negative
Screening and following activity by titer
Pregnancy, SLE and antiphospholipid antibodies, acute viral infections, injection drug use
Uncommon; other treponemal infections such as yaws
blocks.caption: Nontreponemal titers measure activity; treponemal tests measure past or present exposure.

blocks.title: Reading syphilis serology
blocks.text: A pregnant woman has a positive RPR at a titer of 1:2 and a negative TP-PA. A treponemal test is the specific one, so the negative result means this RPR is a biological false positive, which pregnancy alone can cause. Now compare a man with a negative RPR and a positive TP-PA. The treponemal antibody shows past or present infection, while the negative nontreponemal test usually means treated past infection, though very early primary or late latent syphilis can look the same. Third case: an RPR of 1:64 with a positive TP-PA means active infection, and a fourfold or greater fall in titer later indicates response. If secondary syphilis is strongly suspected but a very high antibody level gives a falsely negative undiluted RPR (prozone effect), diluting the serum reveals the reaction.

Both viruses have double-stranded DNA genomes and replicate in the host cell nucleus, but they differ in structure, in how they leave the cell, and in what they do over the long term. HSV-2 kills the cells it replicates in and hides in neurons; HPV completes its life cycle without killing cells and, for high-risk types, can drive malignant transformation.

blocks.title: HSV-2 compared with HPV
rows: Yes; fragile, so spread needs close contact
No; resists drying and survives on surfaces
Lytic: ballooning, multinucleated giant cells, intranuclear (Cowdry A) inclusions
Productive without lysis: koilocytes in upper layers
Latency in sacral sensory ganglia, recurrent outbreaks
Persistent infection; high-risk types can transform cells
Grouped painful vesicles on a red base that become shallow ulcers
blocks.caption: The envelope explains why HSV is fragile outside the body and HPV is hardy.

blocks.title: HSV-2 latency and recurrence
steps: Replication in genital epithelium produces painful vesicles
Virus enters sensory nerve endings
Retrograde axonal transport to sacral dorsal root ganglia
Latency: episomal genome, only latency-associated transcripts made
Stress, fever, or immunosuppression reactivates replication
Anterograde transport returns virus to the same dermatome
blocks.caption: No viral proteins are made during latency, so infected neurons are invisible to CD8 T cells.

blocks.text: The first episode is usually the most severe, with fever, tender inguinal nodes, and many lesions, because there is no prior immunity. Recurrences are milder and occur in the same area. Virus is also shed intermittently from normal-looking skin, which accounts for much transmission. HSV-1 now causes a substantial share of genital herpes; it then becomes latent in sacral ganglia, while oral HSV-1 is latent in the trigeminal ganglion. PCR of lesion fluid is the preferred test.

HPV infects basal keratinocytes but expresses its capsid proteins (L1, L2) and assembles virions only in the differentiating upper layers, so virus is shed with desquamated cells. There is no cell lysis, no viremia, and little inflammation, which lets infection persist. In low-risk types 6 and 11, the E6 and E7 proteins bind p53 and Rb weakly and the genome stays episomal; they cause condyloma acuminatum (exophytic genital warts) and recurrent respiratory papillomatosis. High-risk types 16 and 18 (with others such as 31, 33, and 45) cause most cervical cancers and also anal, oropharyngeal, vulvar, vaginal, and penile carcinomas. Type 16 is the most common type in both squamous carcinoma and adenocarcinoma, while type 18 is relatively more frequent in adenocarcinoma.

blocks.title: High-risk HPV transformation
steps: Viral DNA integrates into the host genome, disrupting E2
Loss of E2 repression increases E6 and E7 expression
E6 targets p53 for ubiquitin-mediated degradation
E7 binds Rb, releasing E2F to drive S phase
Damaged cells keep dividing; mutations accumulate
Dysplasia at the transformation zone progresses to carcinoma
blocks.caption: Loss of Rb function causes p16 to accumulate, a tissue marker of high-risk HPV activity.

blocks.predict: Why do HPV 6 and 11 cause warts but rarely cancer, while 16 and 18 cause cancer?
blocks.explain: Low-risk E6 and E7 bind p53 and Rb weakly and the genome stays episomal under E2 control. High-risk E6 and E7 bind strongly, and integration removes E2 restraint, so p53 and Rb are inactivated.
blocks.check: The transformation flow and the paragraph on low-risk types.

blocks.text: The healthy vagina is acidic. Estrogen causes vaginal squamous cells to store glycogen, lactobacilli break down glycogen products to lactic acid, and the pH stays at about 3.8 to 4.5. Lactobacilli also make hydrogen peroxide and bacteriocins that hold other organisms back. Each cause of vaginitis disturbs this system differently, so pH, odor, and a quick look under the microscope usually identify it.

blocks.title: Distinguishing the common causes of vaginitis
rows: Clue cells on saline wet mount, few neutrophils
Budding yeast and pseudohyphae on KOH preparation
Motile pear-shaped trophozoites on saline wet mount, many neutrophils
blocks.caption: Candida leaves the pH acid; bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis raise it.

blocks.text: Bacterial vaginosis is a shift in flora rather than a classic infection. Lactobacilli decline and Gardnerella vaginalis and anaerobes overgrow. Anaerobic metabolism produces amines such as trimethylamine, putrescine, and cadaverine, which raise the pH and smell fishy, especially when KOH makes them volatile. Gardnerella forms biofilms on squamous cells, creating clue cells. Because there is little tissue invasion, there are few white cells.

Trichomonas vaginalis is a pear-shaped protozoan with four anterior flagella, an undulating membrane, and an axostyle. It exists only as a trophozoite with no cyst form, so it cannot survive long outside the body and spreads sexually. It adheres to and damages squamous epithelium, provoking a strong neutrophil response. Motility is lost as the specimen cools, so a wet mount must be read promptly, and even then it misses many cases; NAAT is more sensitive. Infected men are usually asymptomatic.

Candida albicans is part of normal flora, so candidal vaginitis is usually endogenous rather than sexually transmitted. It grows as budding yeast and, in tissue, forms pseudohyphae (chains of elongated buds with constrictions at the joins) and true hyphae. KOH dissolves epithelial cells and debris so the fungal elements stand out. Overgrowth follows anything that removes lactobacilli or raises glycogen and glucose: antibiotic exposure, pregnancy and high estrogen states, poorly controlled diabetes, and impaired cell-mediated immunity.

blocks.title: Working from pH and microscopy
blocks.text: A discharge sample has a pH of 5.5. That rules out Candida as the sole cause, because candidiasis keeps the normal acid pH, and leaves bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis. The saline wet mount shows many neutrophils but no clue cells. Bacterial vaginosis causes little inflammation, so heavy neutrophils point toward Trichomonas even if no motile organism is seen, since the wet mount often misses it. A NAAT for Trichomonas is the logical next test. If instead the pH were 4.2 with itching and thick white discharge, the KOH preparation would be the slide to examine for pseudohyphae.

sections.title: Haemophilus ducreyi and the TSST-1 superantigen

blocks.text: Haemophilus ducreyi and chancroid

Haemophilus ducreyi is a small gram-negative coccobacillus that lines up in chains and parallel rows on Gram stain, a pattern described as a school of fish. It is fastidious, requires hemin (X factor), and grows only on enriched media, so culture is difficult and NAAT is used where available. It enters through small breaks in genital skin and provokes an intense neutrophil and macrophage response. The result is a soft, painful ulcer with ragged, undermined edges and a gray-yellow purulent base, often with tender, usually one-sided inguinal nodes (buboes) that may suppurate. Chancroid is uncommon in the United States but, like other ulcer diseases, increases HIV transmission.

blocks.title: Genital ulcers compared
rows: Painless, indurated, clean base, usually single
Painful grouped vesicles that become shallow ulcers
Tender, mainly in the first episode
blocks.caption: Pain and induration of the ulcer, together with the node pattern, separate the four classic genital ulcer diseases.

blocks.text: Toxic shock syndrome toxin 1

A conventional protein antigen must be processed into peptides that sit in the groove of an MHC class II molecule, and only T cells whose receptors fit that particular peptide respond, a tiny fraction of the T cell pool. TSST-1, secreted by some strains of Staphylococcus aureus, skips this step. The intact toxin binds the outside of the MHC class II molecule (mainly the alpha chain), away from the peptide groove, and also binds the variable region of the T cell receptor beta chain (V-beta). Every T cell carrying a compatible V-beta segment is activated whatever its peptide specificity, which can be up to about 20% of all T cells.

blocks.title: How TSST-1 causes shock
steps: S. aureus grows on a retained tampon, packing, or wound
TSST-1 is secreted and crosses the mucosa
Toxin links MHC class II to T cell receptor V-beta
A large fraction of T cells activates at once
Massive IL-2, IFN-gamma, TNF, and IL-1 release
Vasodilation and capillary leak: hypotension and multiorgan injury
blocks.caption: The disease is a cytokine storm caused by the toxin, not by invasion of the bloodstream.

blocks.text: The clinical picture follows the cytokines: fever of 38.9 degrees C (102 degrees F) or higher, hypotension, a diffuse macular erythroderma, involvement of three or more organ systems, and desquamation of the palms and soles about 1 to 2 weeks later. Menstrual cases were linked to high-absorbency tampons, which provide air and a near-neutral pH that favor toxin production; nonmenstrual cases follow surgical wounds, nasal packing, and postpartum infection. Blood cultures are usually negative in staphylococcal toxic shock because the bacteria stay local. People who lack antibody to TSST-1 are susceptible, which is why most cases occur in younger patients.

blocks.predict: Why does a superantigen activate thousands of times more T cells than a conventional antigen?
blocks.explain: It ignores peptide specificity. Binding outside the groove to MHC class II and to a V-beta segment shared by many clones activates all those clones, instead of the rare clone that recognizes one peptide.
blocks.check: The TSST-1 paragraph on conventional versus superantigen recognition.

sections.title: Group B streptococcus and the TORCH organisms

blocks.text: Streptococcus agalactiae (group B streptococcus)

Streptococcus agalactiae is a gram-positive coccus in chains, catalase negative, with the Lancefield group B cell wall carbohydrate. It gives a narrow zone of beta-hemolysis and is resistant to bacitracin, which separates it from bacitracin-sensitive group A Streptococcus pyogenes. In the CAMP test, its CAMP factor acts together with the beta-hemolysin of S. aureus to produce an arrowhead of enhanced hemolysis where the two growths meet. It also hydrolyzes hippurate.

It colonizes the lower gastrointestinal and genital tracts of about 10% to 30% of pregnant women, often intermittently. Its main virulence factor is a polysaccharide capsule rich in sialic acid, which recruits the complement regulator factor H and limits C3b deposition, so the organism resists opsonization and phagocytosis. Protection depends on maternal IgG against the capsule, which crosses the placenta mainly in the third trimester; a preterm infant or one whose mother lacks this antibody is poorly defended. Screening is done by rectovaginal culture late in pregnancy because carriage fluctuates and only colonization near delivery predicts exposure.

blocks.title: Neonatal group B streptococcal disease
rows: First week of life, most within 24 hours
Ascending or birth canal exposure; aspiration of infected fluid
Vertical or from caregivers and environment
Preterm birth, membranes ruptured 18 hours or more, intrapartum fever, heavy maternal colonization or GBS bacteriuria, previous affected infant
blocks.caption: Group B streptococcus is a leading cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis; it is a perinatal pathogen, not a TORCH agent.

blocks.text: TORCH organisms

Most TORCH organisms reach the fetus during a maternal infection with a blood-borne phase: they infect the placenta and then the fetal circulation. Infection during organogenesis (weeks 3 to 8) is most likely to cause malformations, while later infection causes growth restriction and inflammation of formed organs. Maternal IgG crosses the placenta through the neonatal Fc receptor but IgM does not, so pathogen-specific IgM in a newborn means the fetus made it in response to its own infection. The O group includes syphilis, varicella-zoster virus, parvovirus B19, Listeria, HIV, and Zika virus, and some lists add others. HSV is the exception: most neonatal HSV is acquired during delivery from genital shedding.

blocks.title: Classic congenital and perinatal infections
rows: Chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, scattered intracranial calcifications; transmission rises later in pregnancy but severity falls
Early: rhinitis, rash including palms and soles, hepatosplenomegaly, osteochondritis. Late: notched incisors, saddle nose, saber shins, interstitial keratitis, deafness
Infects erythroid precursors via P antigen: fetal anemia, high-output heart failure, hydrops
Cataracts, sensorineural deafness, patent ductus arteriosus, blueberry muffin rash from dermal hematopoiesis
Transplacental after primary or recurrent maternal infection
Most common congenital infection: sensorineural hearing loss, periventricular calcifications, microcephaly, petechiae
Skin, eye, and mouth vesicles; encephalitis; disseminated disease
blocks.caption: Congenital CMV is the leading infectious, nongenetic cause of sensorineural hearing loss in children.

integration.text: These organisms connect several Part I disciplines. Microbiology supplies the identifying features, but immunology explains much of the disease: gonococcal antigenic variation and IgA protease defeat mucosal antibody, terminal complement deficiency predisposes to disseminated Neisseria, chlamydial scarring is largely immune mediated, the group B streptococcal capsule recruits factor H, and TSST-1 bypasses antigen processing altogether. Pathology adds the tissue reactions: endarteritis obliterans in syphilis, koilocytes and p53 and Rb inactivation in HPV-driven neoplasia, and placental infection in TORCH disease timed against embryologic organogenesis.

The laboratory findings are tools with limits. Gram stain is reliable for male urethral gonorrhea but not for endocervical specimens or for Chlamydia and Treponema, which it cannot show well; wet mounts miss many Trichomonas infections; nontreponemal tests give false positives; and newborn findings overlap among TORCH agents, so serology, NAAT, and PCR confirm what the pattern suggests. Several infections often coexist, because the same exposures transmit them and genital ulcers ease the entry of other pathogens, including HIV.

summary: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is an oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococcus that uses glucose but not maltose, grows on Thayer-Martin agar, and evades immunity through pilin and Opa variation, IgA1 protease, and sialylated LOS.

Chlamydia trachomatis is obligately intracellular; the elementary body infects and the reticulate body divides; MOMP defines serovars A to C (trachoma), D to K (genital and neonatal), and L1 to L3 (LGV).
Treponema pallidum is too thin for Gram stain, is seen by dark-field microscopy, cannot be grown on standard media, and crosses the placenta at any stage of pregnancy.
Nontreponemal titers (RPR, VDRL) track activity and can be falsely positive; treponemal tests confirm infection and usually stay positive for life.
HSV-2 is an enveloped, lytic dsDNA virus that becomes latent in sacral sensory ganglia and reactivates in the same dermatome.
HPV is a nonenveloped circular dsDNA virus; types 6 and 11 cause warts, while high-risk 16 and 18 E6 and E7 inactivate p53 and Rb and drive carcinoma.
Vaginitis sorts by pH and microscopy: clue cells and amines in bacterial vaginosis, pseudohyphae on KOH with normal pH in Candida, motile flagellates with heavy inflammation in Trichomonas.
Haemophilus ducreyi is a gram-negative coccobacillus in school of fish chains causing a painful soft ulcer, unlike the painless indurated chancre of syphilis.
TSST-1 is a superantigen that links MHC class II to T cell receptor V-beta outside the groove, activating up to about 20% of T cells and causing a cytokine storm.

Group B streptococcus is beta-hemolytic, bacitracin resistant, and CAMP positive, and causes neonatal sepsis and meningitis; most TORCH agents cross the placenta, while neonatal HSV is mainly acquired at delivery.

verify: Neisseria produce acid from carbohydrates by oxidative metabolism; the registry and review books call this fermentation. Confirm the wording NABNE uses.
Group B streptococcal screening is now recommended at 36 0/7 to 37 6/7 weeks (ACOG 2019); older sources give 35 to 37 weeks. This chapter avoids a specific week; confirm what NABNE expects.
Maternal group B streptococcal colonization rates are quoted from about 10% to 30% depending on population and source.
Continuous in vitro culture of Treponema pallidum with rabbit epithelial cells has been reported since 2018; the chapter states only that it cannot be grown on standard media.
The fraction of T cells activated by a superantigen is quoted from about 5% to 20% (sometimes up to 30%) across immunology texts.
Timing windows for gonococcal (2 to 5 days) and chlamydial (5 to 14 days) neonatal conjunctivitis and for chlamydial pneumonia (4 to 12 weeks) vary slightly between sources.

Toxic shock syndrome criteria (fever 38.9 degrees C (102 degrees F) or higher, desquamation, three or more organ systems) follow CDC case definitions, which have been revised; confirm the current version.
The scattered versus periventricular calcification distinction between Toxoplasma and CMV is classic board teaching, but imaging patterns overlap in practice.
The share of cervical cancers attributed to HPV 16 and 18 (about 70%) and the membership of the TORCH Other group vary among sources.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects eponyms such as Fitz-Hugh-Curtis, Cowdry A, Argyll Robertson, and Hutchinson teeth, or only descriptive terms.
